body:
Two major powers in medieval South India

During the 14th century, 2 important states emerged in the Deccan and southern India: the Vijayanagara Empire and the Bahmani Sultanate. They became influential political and military powers and competed for fertile agricultural land, forts, trading routes and access to valuable imports.

The Deccan is the plateau region between northern and southern India. Its rivers, agricultural areas and routes connecting the Arabian Sea with the interior made it strategically important. A ruler who controlled a fertile river valley could collect agricultural revenue, while control over a port or trading route could support commerce and provide access to imported horses and other goods.

Foundation of the 2 states

Vijayanagara was established in the 14th century by the brothers Harihara and Bukka, traditionally dated to 1336. They belonged to the Sangama dynasty, the first ruling dynasty of the empire. The exact foundation date is conventionally given as 1336, although historical accounts retain some uncertainty about it.

The capital was Vijayanagara, identified with present-day Hampi in Karnataka, on the banks of the Tungabhadra River. Vijayanagara means 'city of victory'. The empire eventually exercised authority over extensive parts of southern India, although its boundaries changed with military campaigns and political circumstances.

The Bahmani Sultanate was founded in 1347 by Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah, following a rebellion against the authority of the Delhi Sultanate under Muhammad bin Tughlaq. Its first capital was Gulbarga, also known as Ahsanabad, in present-day Karnataka. The capital was subsequently shifted to Bidar during the 15th century.

FeatureVijayanagara EmpireBahmani Sultanate
FoundationTraditionally 13361347
FounderHarihara and BukkaAlauddin Hasan Bahman Shah
Initial ruling houseSangama dynastyBahmani dynasty
Principal capitalVijayanagara, now HampiGulbarga; later Bidar
Main political regionSouthern peninsulaCentral Deccan

Why their geographical position mattered

The Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers were especially important. The tract between them, known as the Raichur Doab, contained valuable agricultural land and strategically placed forts. It became a major area of conflict between Vijayanagara and the Bahmani rulers and, later, the successor Deccan Sultanates.

Vijayanagara also faced the Gajapati rulers of Odisha to the east and northeast. These relationships involved both warfare and diplomacy. Political competition was not simply a permanent conflict between Hindu and Muslim rulers: rulers also formed alliances, supported claimants in neighbouring kingdoms and adopted useful administrative or architectural practices from one another.

Distinguish the regions

Vijayanagara was based in the southern peninsula, while the Bahmani Sultanate was based in the central Deccan. Their competing interests met particularly in the Raichur Doab and other valuable agricultural and commercial regions.

Prelims focus

  • Harihara and Bukka: traditional founders of Vijayanagara in 1336.
  • Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah: founder of the Bahmani Sultanate in 1347.
  • Vijayanagara's capital: Hampi, Karnataka, on the Tungabhadra.
  • Bahmani capitals: Gulbarga first, Bidar later.
  • Raichur Doab: land between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers.
  • Trap: Hampi and Gulbarga were not capitals of the same kingdom.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Theme 7, 'An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara', pp. 170–172; NIOS, History (315), Lesson 11, sections 11.7–11.8; IGNOU, The Regional Powers: 13th–15th Century, Unit 28, sections 28.1–28.2. Online sources consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: The Rise of Vijayanagara and the Bahmani Sultanate

body:
Political succession and ruling dynasties

Vijayanagara was ruled by a succession of dynasties. Changes in the ruling family did not necessarily mean the end of the empire; military commanders and powerful nobles could replace an established dynasty while continuing to govern the same broad political system.

DynastyApproximate period or transitionImportant association
SangamaFrom the foundation to 1485Harihara and Bukka; first ruling house
Saluva1485–1503Replaced Sangama rulers
TuluvaFrom 1503 into the 16th centuryKrishnadeva Raya
AraviduFrom the later 16th centuryContinuation after the destruction of the old capital

The sequence to remember is Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva and Aravidu. These names identify ruling dynasties, not separate capital cities.

Krishnadeva Raya: expansion and consolidation

Krishnadeva Raya ruled from 1509 to 1529 and belonged to the Tuluva dynasty. He is among the best-known Vijayanagara rulers because his reign combined military success, political consolidation, prosperity and substantial cultural patronage.

His campaigns strengthened Vijayanagara's position against neighbouring powers. He fought the Gajapati rulers of Odisha and the rulers of Bijapur. His victory over Bijapur in the Battle of Raichur in 1520 was particularly significant because the Raichur Doab was a long-contested agricultural and military region.

Military victories strengthened the ruler's authority, but maintaining an empire required more than winning battles. Commanders had to remain loyal, forts had to be defended, agricultural revenue had to be collected and horses had to be obtained for cavalry forces.

Urban and cultural patronage

Krishnadeva Raya contributed to major temple-building projects. At the Virupaksha temple, he commissioned a pillared hall associated with his accession and is credited with constructing the eastern gateway. He also founded a township called Nagalapuram, named after his mother.

He composed the Telugu work Amuktamalyada, which contains ideas about kingship and government. Its discussion of improving harbours and encouraging merchants illustrates a practical connection between trade, military strength and royal policy. Imported horses and valuable goods were useful to a state that maintained large armies and a wealthy court.

Problems after 1529

Following Krishnadeva Raya's death in 1529, his successors faced struggles among political claimants and increasingly powerful military chiefs. The central government had to manage rulers and commanders who controlled substantial local resources. These difficulties contributed to the empire's later instability.

The most destructive military setback came in 1565, when Vijayanagara's forces were defeated at Rakshasi-Tangadi, commonly called the Battle of Talikota. The city was subsequently sacked. Nevertheless, the Aravidu rulers continued to govern from other centres. Thus, the destruction of the capital must be distinguished from the immediate disappearance of the entire political dynasty.

A common chronological confusion

Krishnadeva Raya was neither the founder of Vijayanagara nor a Sangama ruler. He was a Tuluva ruler whose reign began in 1509, long after the empire's traditional foundation in 1336.

Prelims focus

  • Dynastic sequence: Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, Aravidu.
  • Krishnadeva Raya: Tuluva dynasty, 1509–1529.
  • Battle of Raichur: 1520, against Bijapur.
  • Amuktamalyada: Telugu work associated with Krishnadeva Raya.
  • Nagalapuram: township named after his mother.
  • Trap: The Battle of Raichur in 1520 and the Battle of Talikota in 1565 were different events.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Theme 7, sections 2.1–2.2, pp. 172–174; Richard M. Eaton, 'Kiss My Foot, Said the King: Firearms, Diplomacy, and the Battle for Raichur, 1520', Modern Asian Studies, 2009. Online source consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Krishnadeva Raya's reign combined military campaigns with temple and urban patronage.

title: Vijayanagara Dynasties and the Reign of Krishnadeva Raya

body:
The ruler and the territorial administration

The Vijayanagara ruler was commonly called the raya. He stood at the centre of the political system, directed major military campaigns, granted authority to commanders and received revenue and tribute from territories under imperial control.

The empire covered regions with different languages, local traditions and earlier political institutions. Consequently, the government relied on provincial and local authorities as well as officers connected directly to the royal court. Its authority was not exercised everywhere through an identical system of officials.

The importance of the nayakas

Nayakas were powerful military chiefs, often associated with forts, armed followers and control over local territories. Many recognised the authority of Vijayanagara's rulers, although some resisted or rebelled against central control.

A particularly important arrangement was the amara-nayaka system. Under this system, the raya assigned territories to military commanders known as amara-nayakas. The commanders administered these territories and collected taxes and other dues from peasants, craftspeople and traders.

The revenue they collected served several purposes:

  • Maintaining the commander's soldiers and a specified contingent of horses and elephants.
  • Supporting the commander's establishment and local administration.
  • Providing resources for temples and irrigation works.
  • Meeting obligations of tribute and gifts to the central ruler.

How the raya maintained control

The amara-nayakas were expected to show loyalty to the king. They generally sent tribute annually and appeared at the royal court with gifts. The ruler could also transfer commanders from one territory to another. Such transfers were a means of preventing local military authority from becoming entirely independent.

The system therefore combined delegated administration with military obligations. The raya did not have to manage every village directly, but he depended on commanders to supply fighting forces and recognise central authority.

Amara-nayaka system

A Vijayanagara arrangement in which a military commander received responsibility for a territory, collected its revenues, maintained troops and owed tribute and loyalty to the raya.

Village administration and the ayagars

At the village level, administrative and service duties could be performed by officials and hereditary functionaries often discussed under the ayagar system. These included such roles as the village headman, accountant and watchman. They helped manage local records, administration and village services and could receive shares of produce or assignments of land as remuneration.

The ayagar system and the amara-nayaka system should not be confused. Ayagars were associated mainly with village administration and services; amara-nayakas were territorial military commanders with wider revenue and military responsibilities.

Strength and weakness of the system

Delegating power to commanders allowed Vijayanagara to mobilise substantial armies and govern a large territory. However, a commander who controlled soldiers, forts and local revenue could also become a rival to the king. As central power weakened, some nayakas increasingly acted independently. During the 17th century, several established their own kingdoms, contributing to the fragmentation of imperial authority.

Prelims focus

  • Raya: title commonly used for the Vijayanagara ruler.
  • Nayaka: military chief with local territorial influence.
  • Amara-nayaka: commander responsible for a revenue-producing territory and military contingent.
  • Amara-nayakas owed tribute and loyalty to the ruler.
  • Ayagar system: village-level administrative and service functionaries.
  • Trap: An amara-nayaka was not simply a village accountant or watchman.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Theme 7, section 2.3, p. 175; IGNOU, The Delhi Sultanate-II, Unit 27, sections on Vijayanagara kingship, nayaka administration and the ayagar system, pp. 385–392. Online source consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Local taxpayers fund the amara-nayaka, who retains revenue for local needs and owes tribute, gifts, military support and loyalty to the raya.
pictures.caption: Territorial revenue supported both the nayaka's military force and the raya's authority.

title: Vijayanagara Administration: Rayas, Nayakas and Revenue

body:
The Sultan and his officers

The Bahmani Sultanate, founded in 1347, developed an administrative structure influenced by the Delhi Sultanate while adapting to conditions in the Deccan. The Sultan was the supreme political authority. Ministers, military officers, judges and provincial governors assisted him in governing the state.

The wazir was an important minister associated with the central administration. The government had to collect revenue, maintain troops, protect forts, manage provincial officers and respond to powerful nobles who controlled substantial military resources.

Provincial administration: tarafs and tarafdars

The Bahmani territories were divided into provinces called tarafs. A provincial governor was known as a tarafdar. A tarafdar exercised authority over provincial administration and had important military and revenue responsibilities.

Under Muhammad Shah I, the Sultanate was organised into 4 major tarafs associated with Gulbarga, Bidar, Berar and Daulatabad. As the state expanded, large provincial commands became difficult for the centre to supervise.

Two different administrative terms

Amara-nayaka refers to a Vijayanagara territorial military commander. Tarafdar refers to a governor of a Bahmani province. Both held important local power, but they belonged to different states and administrative arrangements.

Mahmud Gawan and the strengthening of central authority

Mahmud Gawan was a prominent Bahmani minister of Persian origin. He became one of the most influential statesmen of the Sultanate during the 15th century. His military campaigns expanded Bahmani influence, while his administrative reforms aimed to limit the excessive independence of provincial governors.

One of his best-known reforms was to reorganise the kingdom's 4 large provinces into 8 smaller provinces. Smaller provincial commands were intended to reduce the concentration of territorial power in the hands of individual governors.

He also restricted governors' authority over forts. Instead of allowing each governor to control all the forts within his province, the system placed more forts under officers appointed by the central government. Certain lands were brought under direct royal control, strengthening the Sultan's access to revenue.

These reforms addressed a central political problem: a governor who controlled a large territory, its revenues and several forts could challenge the Sultan. By dividing provinces and increasing central control over forts and revenue, Gawan sought to make the government more effective.

Military organisation and provincial power

The Bahmani armies employed cavalry, infantry and elephants. Forts were important for defending territory and controlling strategic routes. The use of gunpowder weapons also became part of Deccan warfare. As in Vijayanagara, access to good cavalry horses was an important military concern.

Deccani and Afaqi nobles

Political competition within the Bahmani court included rivalry between groups commonly called the Dakhnis or Deccanis and the Afaqis. The Deccanis were established elites with longer connections to the Deccan, while the Afaqis generally included more recent arrivals from regions such as Iran and Central Asia. These labels referred to competing courtly and political networks, not simply to 2 religious communities.

Mahmud Gawan tried to maintain a balance among influential noble groups. Nevertheless, factional conflicts continued. He was executed in 1481 after accusations made against him. His death weakened a ministerial authority that had sought to restrain powerful provincial nobles, and the Sultanate subsequently experienced increasing fragmentation.

Prelims focus

  • Taraf: province of the Bahmani Sultanate.
  • Tarafdar: provincial governor.
  • The early Sultanate had 4 major tarafs.
  • Mahmud Gawan reorganised the provinces from 4 to 8.
  • His reforms increased central control over forts and royal lands.
  • Trap: Mahmud Gawan was a Bahmani minister, not a Vijayanagara ruler.

[Sources: IGNOU, The Regional Powers: 13th–15th Century, Unit 28, sections 28.4–28.6, pp. 56–58; IGNOU, The Delhi Sultanate-II, Unit 27, sections on Bahmani administration and Mahmud Gawan's reforms, pp. 393–396; NIOS, History (315), Lesson 11, section 11.7. Online sources consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Mahmud Gawan's reforms reduced the territorial and military concentration of provincial authority.

title: Bahmani Government and Mahmud Gawan's Administrative Reforms
